newsitem.title: GERMANY: German upper house rejects part of Kohl's tax bill.
newsitem.headline: German upper house rejects part of Kohl's tax bill.

text.p: Germany's upper house of parliament, dominated by the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), on Friday rejected a bill aimed at reforming the nation's tax system and stimulating investment and jobs creation.

The reforms, backed by Chancellor Helmut Kohl's ruling coalition, including plans to cut taxes by around 30 billion marks in the next two years, will now have to wait until the summer, probably July, when a mediation committee will try to hammer out a compromise between the two sides.
The bill included plans to cut the unpopular solidarity tax surcharge, levied after unification in 1990 to fund development of the former communist east, to 5.5 percent from 7.5 percent.

But Kohl's coalition has since said the solidarity surcharge will be removed from the package of tax reforms in future, because it does not need the approval of the Bundesrat upper house to become law.

The Bundesrat, representing Germany's 16 regional states, must give its approval for bills that are relevant to the affairs of the states. The revenues from the solidarity surcharge do not go to regional state coffers.
The government will, however, need Bundesrat approval for the other planned tax cuts in the bill.
These include cutting corporate taxes to 40 percent from 45-47 percent, but will not include government proposals to slash the top 53 percent rate of income tax.

SPD-ruled states say that government plans to cut taxes are not mirrored by plans to increase revenues elsewhere, a sensitive issue after Bonn announced on Thursday it faced an 18 billion mark ($10.6 billion) tax revenue shortfall.
But they expect that both sides will try to reach a compromise in the mediation committee due to meet this summer, which will also discuss plans to cut income tax rates.
